R. 11 China. 12 13 14 15 * Corresponding authors: Shaofan Li, Jinyang Jiang 16 17 18 19 Abstract 20 CO2 sequestration in concrete is crucial to relieve the environmental burden, while the 21 carbonation mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we explored the carbonation dynamics of alite 22 hydrates through electron microscopy. We discovered that calcite is the main phase of carbonate 23 crystals throughout the entire carbonation period in alite system. The shape evolution of calcite 24 crystals was captured: our observations revealed that the spindle carbonates initially formed on 25 the C-S-H substrate and then transformed into rhombohedrons; Intermediate states such as 26 polyhedral particles and layered rhomboids were also observed. Based on our quantitative 27 calculations, the growth rate of calcite particles was determined to be approximately 0.2 μm/day, 28 which may be affected by the relative concentration between calcium ions and the CO2 source. A 29 direct relation between the microstructure and mechanical properties of calcite was uncovered 30 using atomic force microscopy. Furthermore, we found that the morphology development of 31 calcite crystals during carbonation could be explained by the surface energy variation of different 32 facets. This work suggests a unique approach to track carbonation kinetics and provides new 33 opportunities to unveil the underlying carbonation mechanisms at the nanoscale. 34 35 36 Keywords 37 Carbonation dynamics; Calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H); Calcite; Electron microscopy; Atomic 38 force microscopy; Mechanical properties 39 40 41 42 43 44 45 46

1 1. Introduction 2 Concrete is a vital building block of the urbanizing world, and it is the most consumed material 3 by mass except for water. Owing to its large-scale use, cement and concrete production results in 4 substantial emissions of greenhouse gases with an increased environmental burden [1]. Portland 5 cement production releases a tremendous quantity of CO2 into the atmosphere because of the 6 calcination of the limestone decomposition and fuel combustion, responsible for 8-9% of the 7 global anthropogenic CO2 emissions [2]. Fortunately, the cement hydration products can 8 gradually reabsorb atmospheric CO2 through a natural reversal process--carbonation. It is a 9 physiochemical process that involves the diffusion of CO2 into the porous hydrates and the 10 reactions in the presence of pore water [3,4]. Although the CO2 uptake by cement carbonation 11 takes place over the life cycle of cement materials, the proportion of sequestrated carbon 12 annually is still trivial [5,6], which necessitates strategies to limit the environmental impact 13 towards sustainable concrete. 14 Reduction of CO2 emissions by adopting “carbon capture and storage” technologies in cement 15 production is becoming an attractive and active research area. One strategy being used is 16 applying accelerated carbonation to enhance the properties of recycled coarse aggregates [7]. It 17 was reported that mechanical properties [8] and durability [9] of concrete were significantly 18 improved due to a densification of the interfacial transition zone of aggregates after the 19 carbonation treatment [10]. Alternative approaches focus on the CO2 curing of concrete with 20 optimized operation factors, such as CO2 pressure, curing time and relative humidity [11–13]. 21 The results were promising that the mechanical properties of the treated specimens were 22 comparable to those of steam curing [14,15]. Some of the CO2-cured concrete blocks even 23 exhibited lower drying shrinkage and better dimensional stability [16]. Both solutions can be 24 implemented within the next decade and beyond to consume a large amount of CO2. In fact, 25 carbonation is a pervasive process in synthetic, geochemical, and biological systems. Such 26 explorations advance the sustainability of cement production and also impact many other 27 research fields, including biomineralization [17], rechargeable Li-CO2 batteries [18], novel CO2 28 sequestration methods [19], etc. 29 The chemical and microstructural phenomena throughout cement carbonation are sophisticated 30 because of the complexity of the cement system [20,21], making it difficult to resolve the 31 individual mechanisms or the dominating parameters. Alite (3CaO·SiO2, with minor foreign ions) 32 is the primary component of Portland cement (50-70%) [22]. It controls the early-age hydration 33 kinetics in the formation of Portlandite and C-S-H. Due to its simple chemical composition, it 34 has been frequently employed in the study of hydration/carbonation mechanisms [23,24]. 35 Understanding such carbonation mechanisms, therefore significantly challenges the experimental 36 designs and characterization techniques. Existing knowledge focuses on the mechanisms of long- 37 term carbonation or accelerated carbonation with concentrated CO2 [25,26]. However, the 38 underlying mechanisms of carbonation reactions are not yet fully understood. This lack of 39 understanding of morphological evolution, reaction kinetics, etc., which may hinder future 40 developments in CO2 sequestration technologies. 41 In this work, we investigated the carbonation of alite hydrates, the major product in cement 42 hydration, using electron microscopy. The carbonate crystals were successfully identified 43 through electron diffraction and chemical mapping. We captured the morphological evolution of 44 carbonates, compromising the shape transformation and particle size growth during the entire 45 carbonation process. The kinetics, such as the growth rate and concentration variance, were also 46

Materials and Methodologies 5 Synthesis of alite. Alite was prepared in the laboratory according to the procedures reported by 6 Dvořák [27]. Instead, calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and high purity quartz powder (SiO2), 7 purchased from Sigma Aldrich, were used as raw materials in our synthesis. The final product 8 was examined using powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) to check its crystallinity and identify its 9 crystal structure. 10 Scanning electron microscopy (SEM). FEI Inspect F50 with a Schottky field emission source 11 was employed to observe the alite hydration at different time. The microscope was operated in 12 secondary electron (SE) mode at 10 keV. Note that the hydrate sample was coated by a ~10 nm 13 gold film to avoid charging issues before SEM characterization. Hitachi S-4800 with a cold field 14 emission electron source was applied for the carbonation experiments. All the specimens were 15 imaged in secondary electron (SE) mode at 3 keV. Also, this microscope installs a Bruker 16 Quantax EDS system, which allows for X-ray spectroscopy. To determine the element ratios, we 17 conducted measurements at multiple points, analyzing at least 30 points for each sample. 18 Transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The carbonation experiments were conducted on 19 Tecnai T20 at 200 keV. This microscope was equipped with a LaB6 filament, a Bruker EDS 20 detector, and an Orius SCD200D wide-angle CCD camera, enabling conventional imaging, 21 diffraction, and microanalysis. The FEI ThemIS microscope was used to characterize the 22 elemental composition of the alite hydrates and carbonates. The microscope was operated at 300 23 keV with the Bruker SuperX energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detector, allowing for 24 rapid chemical identification. 25 Experimental setups for carbonation. We developed a new sample preparation method to 26 observe the carbonation dynamics of alite hydrates at the nanoscale through electron microscopy. 27 As illustrated in Figure 1, the alite hydrates were prepared by dilute hydration for 12 hours. Note 28 that dilute hydration of C3S is a standard method in cement hydration study [28]. Although the 29 hydration of alite was controlled at a high water to solid (w/s) ratio of 100:1, the products were 30 still representative with respective to ordinary cement pastes in the similar morphology and 31 chemical composition [29–31]. Such a high w/s ratio can also avoid the precipitation of 32 portlandite, which can significantly simplify the complexity of the hydration system [32]. The 33 hydration products were dropcast on a TEM copper grid (Figure 1B), and we stopped the 34 hydration using the freeze-drying method (Figure 1C). In consequence, the copper gird was 35 transferred to the carbonation chamber at ambient conditions (Figure 1D): (1) ~25 oC; (2) 1 atm; 36 (3) 50%-55% relative humidity; (4) 300-500 ppm CO2 concentration was maintained throughout 37 the carbonation experiment. After carbonation at a desired time, the specimen was transferred to 38 the electron microscope for direct observation. We utilized TEM as the primary probe during the 39 early-stage carbonation due to its exceptional spatial resolution. However, once the calcite 40 particles grew larger than approximately 3 μm, it is challenging to image them using TEM, and 41 therefore SEM characterization became dominant. 42 43

1 3.2. Carbonation of hydrated alite 2 After a continuous alite hydration for 12 hours, the sample is then subjected to carbonation. 3 (Figure 1). In Figure 3, spindle carbonates growing on C-S-H substrates are discovered after 4 one-day carbonation of the hydrated alite. The alite is not sufficiently hydrated exhibiting an 5 unhydrated core and a C-S-H shell (Figure 3A). We found that the C-S-H outer layer is very 6 porous considering the open space in a dilute environment [30]. In contrast, the carbonate 7 crystals possess a high density, and they are relatively uniform at a size of ~1 μm, as the darker 8 contrast from the TEM image implies a bigger density and thickness. The growth of carbonate 9 crystals depends on the C-S-H matrix since it provides the calcium sources and nucleation sites. 10 We found that the carbonates are prone to form at the C-S-H surface. Carbonation reactions on 11 the surfaces are dominated during the initial period considering C-S-H matrix hinders the CO2 12 penetration and transport. 13 The carbonates were resolved as calcite based on the element mapping in Figure 3B and the 14 diffraction pattern in Figure 3C. Various carbonate polymorphs can form at different conditions. 15 For example, vaterite is dominated in synthesized C-S-H at accelerated carbonation conditions 16 (~30,000 ppm CO2) while calcite is the main product in nature carbonation (~400 ppm CO2) [48]. 17 This is consistent with our results that calcite crystals were primarily found. However, the 18 carbonation products can be more complex in cement pastes because of the variety of hydration 19 products and some foreign ions such as Mg2+ may alter the mineralogy of carbonates [49]. 20 Basically, kinds of carbonates including calcite, aragonite, vaterite, and amorphous carbonates 21 observed [50]. Note that the spindle carbonates are rich in calcium and carbon with the elements 22 uniformly distributed. The silicon signal can hardly be detected, implying that only calcium ions 23 participate in the carbonation reaction without silicon incorporated. 24 25

We regraded the layered carbonate rhombohedron as one transition state during the carbonation 1 process. These particles can transform into perfect rhombohedrons after carbonation for 30 days, 2 in Figure 6A. Giant calcite rhombohedrons over 10 μm were noticed with sharp edges. These 3 crystals nucleate on the C-S-H matrix, grow into calcite islands, finally develop into 4 rhombohedral particles, even larger than the C-S-H substrate. Rhombohedral calcite is a typical 5 morphology besides the spindle one [63]. In our previous work [51], the rhombohedral shape is 6 related to a high relative concentration between CO2 and calcium ions, i.e., a big c(CO32- 7 )/c(Ca2+). Considering that a large amount of CO2 gas is steadily fed into the system, while the 8 calcium from C-S-H gel is gradually consumed, the CO2 molecules will be excessive at late stage, 9 leading to a high c(CO32-)/c(Ca2+), which may promote to the formation of calcite 10 rhombohedrons. Rhombohedral calcite is commonly discovered in cementitious materials after 11 carbonation because of the sufficient exposure in CO2 curing and long-term carbonation. In 12 addition, the facets of the rhombohedron were identified {0 1 -1 -4} in Figure 6B. From the 13 aspect of crystallography, these low index facets terminated by carbonate groups are stable with 14 lower surface energy. The facets intersect together at an angle of 75o, which is also a significant 15 clue in the rhombohedral calcite. Here, we have identified calcite as the predominant phase, 16 although it’s possible that phase transformations could occur among various carbonate phases 17 during the carbonation process [58], particularly in the presence of impurities within the system 18 [64]. Therefore, it’s important to consider the potential for phase changes when studying 19 carbonation reactions. 20 21 3.3. Carbonation kinetics 22 We unveiled the carbon kinetics of alite hydrates using electron microscopy. The growth of 23 carbonate particles as a function of time was investigated in Figure 7A, at the average growth 24 rate of 0.2 μm/day. In detail, the carbonation at the microscale can be divided into two periods 25 depending on the growth rates of carbonates. For example, the early stage of carbonation is 26 relatively slow at 0.14 μm/day, which is dominated by surface reactions. The carbonates exhibit 27 spindle shape with lateral elongation and texture densification before 14 days. After that, the 28 carbonation is accelerated by 2 times at 0.3 μm/day, governed by the mass transfer of CO2. A 29 rapid growth of calcite rhombohedrons is predominated during this period. Although our work 30 focuses on the hydrated alite carbonation, it deepens the understanding of nanoscale carbonation 31 mechanisms, which also offers opportunities for manipulating the carbonation process through 32 crystal growth in cement and concrete systems. 33 The morphological evolution of carbonates was captured using electron microscopy (Figure 7B): 34 The major phase of carbonate particles was calcite with identical diffraction patterns. Spindle 35 calcite particles on the C-S-H surface grew into a polyhedral shape; and subsequently transform 36 into layered or perfect rhombohedrons after a sufficient carbonation for 30 days. Such shape 37 evolution at different carbonation periods can be explained by the relative concentration theory 38 proposed in our previous work [51]. According to our “concentration theory”, c(CO32-)/c(Ca2+), 39 governs the shape variations (Figure 7C): spindle calcite is synthesized at a lower relative 40 concentration, i.e., c(CO32-)/c(Ca2+) = 0.8, while rhombohedral calcite is formed at c(CO32- 41 )/c(Ca2+) = 1.0 [51]. 6 Figure 7. Kinetics of carbonation of alite hydrates. (A) The size of carbonate particles as a 7 function of carbonation time. The average size is calculated based on TEM and SEM images. 8 Morphological evolution (B) as a function of carbonation time and (C) with different c(CO32- 9 )/c(Ca2+). 10 11 The development of facets on calcite crystals during carbonation can be explained by surface 12 energy equilibrium. Initially, spindle calcite may have many facets, but those with higher surface 13 energies become unstable and disappear over time as the crystal undergoes carbonation. This 14 process minimizes the total surface energy, resulting in the formation of a final rhombohedral 15 calcite crystal with predominantly low-indexed facets. For example, the crystal may be 16 composed of {0 1 -1 4} facets, which have a lower surface energy. In detail, the exposed facets 17 of spindle calcite were resolved using X-ray methods [72,73], and the crystal can be represented 18 by a polyhedron terminated by the resolved facets (Figure 8A). In Figure 8B, the spindle calcite 19 crystal is cleaved by the facets including the {0 1 -1 4}, {0 1 -1 8}, {2 1 -3 4} and {1 1 -2 0} 20 facets. This is consistent with our findings of the exposed surfaces such as the {0 1 -1 4} in 21 Figure 3, the {2 1 -3 4} in Figure 4, and the {1 1 -2 0} in Figure 5. Here, we applied first- 22 principles DFT calculations to determine the corresponding surface energy. 23 Table 2 shows that the {0 1 -1 4} facet has the lowest surface energy at 44.3 meV/Å2, which is 24 half that of the other facets exposed on the spindle calcite. This suggests that the {0 1 -1 4} facet 25 is the most stable and may dominate during facet development throughout the carbonation 26 process. Molecular dynamics simulations have also reported similar conclusions [74]. Our 27 experimental findings are in agreement with the theory of surface energy, as the calcite 28 rhombohedron is constructed primarily from the {0 1 -1 4} facet (Figure 6B). Conclusions 9 In this work, we employed electron microscopy to investigate the carbonation process of alite 10 hydrates. The carbonation products were identified, and the kinetics including morphological 11 evolution was monitored at different periods. Some conclusions can be obtained as follows: 12 (1) We designed a full series of microscopic characterization methods to investigate the 13 carbonation process of alite hydrates. This protocol provides a powerful research tool in 14 probing dynamic carbonation reactions at nanoscale. 15 (2) The main phase of carbonates was identified as calcite throughout the entire carbonation 16 process. The carbonation kinetics was examined at the growth rate of 0.2 μm/day. 17 (3) The morphological evolution of calcite was captured. The spindle crystal could grow into a 18 polyhedral shape, then develop into a perfect rhombohedron. Such process was governed by 19 the relative concentration, c(CO32-)/c(Ca2+). The adsorption of ions and surface energy 20 variations are responsible for the facet growth of calcite particles. 21 22 This work offers an in-depth understanding of the nanoscale mechanisms of carbonation in the 23 alite hydrates system, which sheds light on the calcite shape-control method and future design of 24 advanced carbonation techniques. 25 26 Acknowledgments 27 J. Determining the crystal facet based on electron diffraction 5 The calcite facets can be determined based on its corresponding electron diffraction pattern. The 6 SAED pattern can be interpreted as the central projection of a spherical (Ewald sphere) cut 7 through the reciprocal lattice into real space. In the diffraction patterns, V(hkil) is a diffraction vector of the reciprocal lattice, 9 whose direction is perpendicular to the corresponding set of diffracting lattice planes, and length 10 is the reciprocal of the lattice plane spacing distance [79]. The crystal surfaces can be determined 11 by identifying the planes in SAED that perpendicular to the diffraction vector. 12 13
